analysis.title: US Economic Weekly: Midterms FAQs
key_insights: BofA does not expect the midterm outcome to meaningfully change its economic outlook through 2028, because legislative scope is limited under any result. Deficits should stay near 6% of GDP, give or take a few tenths.

Baseline is Democrats flipping the House while Republicans keep the Senate. That produces gridlock with little major legislation beyond a modest defense supplemental that includes some Democratic priorities such as healthcare spending.

A Republican sweep is the most consequential case for growth. BofA expects a substantially larger defense reconciliation package than House Republicans' Reconciliation 3.0 bill, lifting growth by roughly 10-20bp in each of the next two years. The administration has requested $500bn in additional defense funding and BofA doubts Congress approves the full amount.

A Democratic sweep differs from a split Congress mainly through control of nominations. Democrats could block or shape Fed, judiciary and other appointments, potentially producing more moderate nominees or vacant seats.

Risk of a lame-duck Republican reconciliation push on defense spending is judged low. The agenda is crowded with permitting reform and appropriations, and Senate Republicans failed to coalesce around the Reconciliation 3.0 package the House passed this summer.

AI regulation is a downside risk under unified Democratic control, but BofA assumes most significant measures would face a presidential veto. State and local rules on zoning, permitting and development agreements are the more important constraint on data centers. BofA sees them slowing construction at the margin and raising costs rather than derailing the investment cycle.

BofA expects the administration to pivot toward foreign policy, trade and deregulation, where executive authority matters more than Congress. This could bring bouts of higher policy uncertainty, but far smaller than the spike after Liberation Day. A more aggressive deregulatory push is expected in finance and power.

Fed call changed: BofA still expects two more hikes but now at a quarterly pace, in Dec '26 and Mar '27, with a terminal rate of 4.25-4.5% held through end-2027. Main risk is that moving slower lets the Fed fall behind the curve, so 25-50bp of extra hikes relative to base case cannot be ruled out. Alternatively, favorable base effects in core PCE early next year could lead the Fed to stop after one more hike in Dec '26.

Oct jobs preview: BofA forecasts payrolls +75k (private +70k) vs consensus 65k and 29k in Sep. The unemployment rate is expected to stay at 4.2%, with participation down about a tenth. A larger drop in participation could push the rate to 4.1%. Downside risks are the recent slowdown in weekly ADP and potentially unfavorable seasonals.

3Q GDP advance came in at 3.4% q/q saar vs 3.2% consensus. Final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, consumer spending rose 3.8% and nonresidential capex rose 12.7%, led by equipment and IPP. Residential investment and net exports weighed on growth.
Sep core PCE was in line at 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, and headline PCE was 0.5% m/m and 3.6% y/y. BofA's bottom line is that the economy is robust and inflation is too high.

The Fed held at its Oct 28 meeting with the midpoint at 3.875%. Fed speakers in October skewed hawkish, and several (Collins, Williams, Logan, Musalem, Waller) have signaled further hikes. Bowman and Jefferson counseled patience. Chair Warsh declined to prejudge meetings and said financial conditions are tighter but not tight.

Card spending per household was up 6.0% y/y in the week ending Oct 24, and 4.8% excluding gas. Gas spending was up 25.5% y/y, and online retail was up 8.3%. Furniture (-5.3%) and department stores (-2.2%) declined.

Core views: BofA forecasts 2.6% 4Q/4Q GDP growth in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027. Core PCE should finish 2026 slightly above 3% and reach 2.5% next year. Job growth averages 70k/mo in 2026 and about 60k in 2027-28, with unemployment at 4.1% through 2027.

BofA's rate forecasts: 10-year Treasury at 5.00% by Dec '26 (spot 4.94%), 2-year at 5.00% (spot 4.60%), and 30-year at 5.25% (spot 5.30%). EUR-USD is forecast at 1.15 by Dec '26 and USD-JPY at 152 (spot 157.68).

sector_views.rationale: State and local regulation is likely to slow construction at the margin and raise development costs, but is not expected to derail the broader data-center investment cycle.

A Republican sweep would likely bring a substantially larger deficit-financed defense reconciliation package. The administration has requested $500bn in additional funding, though BofA doubts the full amount passes.

tension_points.bull_case: BofA's base case is two quarterly-pace hikes (Dec '26, Mar '27) to 4.25-4.5% with solid growth and a roughly balanced labor market. Hawkish officials such as Logan (50bp or more) and Waller (75bp total) support further tightening.
tension_points.bear_case: By moving slower the Fed could fall behind the curve and have to hike 25-50bp more. In the opposite scenario, y/y core PCE rolls off on favorable base effects and the Fed stops after one more hike in Dec '26.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Favorable base effects pulling y/y core PCE down early next year would lead the Fed to stop after just one more hike in Dec '26.

tension_points.bull_case: A Republican sweep would bring a larger defense reconciliation package, adding roughly 10-20bp to growth and potentially a risk-on market reaction through wealth effects.
tension_points.bear_case: Gridlock means little legislation and no material change to growth, and a Democratic sweep could bring AI restrictions and more control over Fed nominations.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Republican push to pass defense spending through reconciliation in the lame duck session would make the outlook look like a Republican sweep.

theme_stances.key_argument: The midterm outcome is unlikely to meaningfully alter the economic outlook because limited legislation is likely under any result.
theme_stances.evidence: Midterms are unlikely to be a gamechanger

theme_stances.key_argument: Growth is solid, inflation is too high and policy is too easy, so two more hikes are coming at a quarterly pace.
theme_stances.evidence: we still expect two more hikes, but they are now likely to arrive at a quarterly pace

theme_stances.key_argument: State and local rules are likely to slow construction at the margin and raise costs rather than derail the investment cycle.
theme_stances.evidence: State and local regulation should remain the more important constraint to watch.
